Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making eye contact with other people

I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

vignette: Alicia had been a bank teller for five years when she was kidnapped and tortured by her ex-boyfriend's associates. The incident lasted only 48 hours, but its impact on her life has been lasting. During those two days, Alicia was repeatedly beaten, threatened with further violence if she didn't reveal personal details about her new partner, and subjected to degrading comments and gestures that still make her skin crawl. When people around her express anger, even calmly, Alicia is instantly transported back to the room where she was held captive. She remembers the sound of muffled yelling outside, the feeling of being completely at the mercy of her captors, and the sensation of her heart racing in anticipation of what would happen next. Even if it's just a colleague raising their voice to emphasize a point or a family member disagreeing with her husband, Alicia feels like she's back in that room, her senses on high alert. She avoids making eye contact with other people because when she looks into someone's eyes, she can't shake the feeling of being watched. She's certain that they're judging her, waiting for her to slip up so they can pounce. At work, this has made it difficult for Alicia to connect with customers; she keeps her gaze down and fumbles through transactions, all the while thinking about how much safer it would be if she just didn't have to deal with people at all. Alicia's also begun overanalysing every detail of the event, replaying conversations in her head, wondering what she could've done differently to prevent it. She'll spend hours poring over memories of that time, trying to make sense of why this happened to her and how she can avoid anything like it in the future. As a distraction from these thoughts, Alicia has turned to compulsive spending. She's always been someone who saves money carefully, but lately, she finds herself buying things on impulse - clothes, jewelry, expensive meals out with friends. It's as if by treating herself to something nice, she can momentarily forget about the terror that still grips her. The smallest sounds make Alicia jump; a sudden noise in an otherwise quiet space sends her heart racing and has her scanning the room for potential threats. She's developed this startle response because during those two days of captivity, every creak of the floor or rustle of fabric seemed to signal something terrible was about to happen. Silence is just as unsettling; Alicia can't shake the feeling that in quiet moments, danger lurks just around the corner, waiting for its moment to strike. At night, she finds herself waking with a start, checking the room frantically to make sure everything is still and safe before lying back down, her heart still pounding. When memories of the event return, Alicia feels overwhelmed by emotion; it's as if the entire experience comes flooding back at once - every sense on high alert, every sensation and sound and smell instantly vivid. Sometimes this happens without warning, triggered by something in her surroundings that she can't quite pinpoint but knows is connected to those terrible days. Alicia's husband has been trying to get her to open up more about what happened, but the thought of sharing these memories - of reliving them all over again - is almost too much for her. She feels like she's barely holding on as it is; one wrong move and everything will come crashing down around her. It was only when Alicia found herself avoiding intimacy with her husband, unable to bear even the thought of being close to him without feeling a wave of panic wash over her, that she realized she needed help. The memories still feel so raw, so present, that Alicia's not sure how much more she can take on her own; all she knows is that something has to change before it's too late.
